newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - Focus on US data, German unemployment.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Focus on US data, German unemployment.

text.p: U.S. economic data will again provide the main focus for financial markets in the week ahead as players try to gauge when the Federal Reserve is likely to raise its funds rate again, analysts said on Friday.
European attention will be held by German unemployment data, and markets will also be looking for possible rate cuts.

"Next week looks pretty quiet," said Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe in London. "The trend has been, and will be, centred on the U.S. partly because (Europe) is in a bit of data vacuum."
The key U.S. economic fundamentals will be provided by the March producer price index and retail sales data due on Friday.
Fishwick said the market would be looking at these figures for evidence of the U.S. economy starting to slow after the Fed raised its funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25.

But he said while in the past the market had attached quite a lot of significance to PPI, it should now wean itself off these numbers and instead look at high frequency, forward looking indicators, such as weekly confidence indicators.

"The Fed had greatly devalued the pipeline inflation data in the way it has almost exclusively concentrated on the real economy," he said. "The problem is these forward looking data are horribly volatile so it will be a rather frustrating task."
In Germany, many analysts were looking for a fall in the unemployment figures on Tuesday reflecting a possible turnaround in the German economy.

Tom Rayner, economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull in London, said unemployment was a two-fold problem for Germany, not only because of the weak economy, but also because of structural problems in the labour market.
"We are going for a fall of 20,000 in unemployment for March which might underline that the economy has turned and maybe we have seen the worst on the unemployment side as well," he said.

"In terms of Bunds, that could be a little bit negative. Bond markets being what they are, like to see people out of work unfortunately," said Rayner adding that a fall in the unemployment level would also help Germany achieve the three percent EU economic and monetary union government deficit target.

"The easier that becomes for Germany the more likely it is that Germany is going to be very tough on everyone else," he said. "If Germany can't make three percent they are going to find it harder to block countries like Italy, so it has implications for the peripheral markets as well."
Rob Hayward, economic adviser at BankAmerica in London, said the focus elsewhere in Europe was turning towards the prospect of interest rate cuts in Italy, Spain, Portugal and France.

"We are looking for good inflation figures from France and the strong probability that the Bank of France will trim the intervention rate when they meet on Thursday," he said. "And we should get decent Spanish inflation figures at the end of the week which would set the market up probably for a cut the following week."
In Britain, Rayner said the markets would be looking at February manufacturing output figures on Wednesday for any indication that the strength of sterling was damaging the manufacturing industry.

"It looks like we have become competitive enough at this stage to maintain our overseas position and domestic demand is clearly strengthening so that should be a fairly key influence for the UK," he said. "We are looking for a firm manufacturing number which should keep the pressure on for a UK rate rise."
Bank of England governor Eddie George is due to have his regular monthly meeting with Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke on Thursday.
"This will be the last meeting before the election and you would be a brave man to say anything would happen there," said Rayner.
